concept.name: Reactive Streams Backpressure

relationships.description: Connects Reactive Streams Backpressure to python concurrency nogil in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Reactive Streams backpressure is a non-blocking, pull-based flow-control protocol where downstream consumers explicitly signal how many items (`request(n)`) they can process, preventing fast producers from overwhelming slow consumers.
spark.keyTakeaway: Never bridge async producers and slow consumers with unbounded queues; use bounded `request(n)` demand signaling (e.g., Project Reactor, RSocket, gRPC HTTP/2 flow control) and define an explicit overflow strategy (`drop`, `latest`, or `error`) at non-backpressured boundaries.

concept.whyItMatters: In high-throughput async pipelines, a 10x speed mismatch between a network socket (100k msg/s) and a database sink (10k writes/s) silently fills unbounded `LinkedBlockingQueue`s until the JVM hits `OutOfMemoryError` or GC death spirals. Backpressure turns memory bloat into controlled upstream slowdowns.
whenToUse: Streaming pipelines connecting fast ingress (Kafka, WebSockets, SSE, HTTP/2) to slower I/O sinks (PostgreSQL, Elasticsearch, ML inference).
Non-blocking JVM or actor systems (Project Reactor, Akka/Pekko Streams, RxJava) where threads must never block on `queue.put()`.
Cross-service streaming protocols (RSocket `REQUEST_N`, gRPC HTTP/2 `WINDOW_UPDATE`) requiring end-to-end flow control.
whenNotToUse: Simple request-response CRUD endpoints where single-item HTTP timeouts and connection pool limits already bound concurrency.
Live telemetry or mouse-move streams that cannot be slowed down at the source—here you must explicitly drop, sample, or conflate (`onBackpressureLatest`) rather than propagating demand.
Low-volume batch jobs (< 1,000 items) where reactive operator complexity hurts readability without measurable memory or throughput benefit.
keyPoints: Reactive Streams standardizes 4 interfaces (`Publisher`, `Subscriber`, `Subscription`, `Processor`) with dynamic push-pull semantics: `Subscription.request(n)` pulls demand, `Subscriber.onNext(item)` pushes data.
Demand is cumulative: calling `request(10)` then `request(5)` grants 15 total items; the publisher must never emit more than total unfulfilled demand.
Dynamic push-pull avoids the RTT penalty of pure 1-by-1 polling: consumers prefetch batches (e.g., Reactor's `Queues.SMALL_BUFFER_SIZE = 256`) and replenish at 75% consumption.
Operators like `flatMap` and `publishOn` maintain internal prefetch buffers; misconfiguring concurrency (`flatMap(..., maxConcurrency)`) can still spike memory.
Non-backpressured sources (e.g., `Sinks.many()`, UDP sockets, UI events) require explicit overflow strategies: `BUFFER` (bounded), `DROP`, `LATEST`, or `ERROR`.

examples.title: Kafka-to-Postgres Ingestion Pipeline in Project Reactor
examples.scenario: A Spring WebFlux + Reactor Kafka consumer reads 50,000 events/sec, but batched PostgreSQL R2DBC inserts top out at 12,000 rows/sec.
examples.outcome: Using `bufferTimeout(500, 100ms)` with `limitRate(256)` propagates `request(n)` upstream, pausing Kafka partition polling automatically when Postgres slows down—holding heap usage flat at ~180 MB instead of OOMing.

examples.title: gRPC Streaming Over HTTP/2 Flow Control
examples.scenario: A Python ML client streams 10 MB/s of video frames over gRPC bidirectional streaming to a GPU worker that processes frames at 4 MB/s.
examples.outcome: HTTP/2 per-stream flow control (`WINDOW_UPDATE` frames on a 64 KB–1 MB window) pauses the client's `send()` when the server stops reading from the stream, preventing unbounded server-side buffering.

tradeOffs.factor: Prefetch Batch Size (`request(n)`) vs. Memory & Latency
tradeOffs.pro: Larger `n` (e.g., 256) amortizes synchronization and network RTTs for high throughput.
tradeOffs.con: Larger `n` increases per-stream memory buffers and delays head-of-line cancellation or fairness across multiplexed streams.

tradeOffs.pro: Propagating demand guarantees zero data loss for durable queues and files.
tradeOffs.con: Can stall upstream producers or exhaust client sockets; real-time market tickers prefer `onBackpressureLatest` to stay fresh.

tradeOffs.pro: Reactive Streams minimize thread count and enforce explicit bounded buffers end-to-end.
tradeOffs.con: Steeper debugging stack traces; simple I/O services may get cleaner code with Virtual Threads + bounded `Semaphore`/`BlockingQueue`.

failureModes.name: Unbounded `onBackpressureBuffer()` OOM
failureModes.description: Inserting an unbounded buffer operator between a fast hot source and a stalled sink absorbs memory until the process crashes with `OutOfMemoryError`.
failureModes.mitigation: Always specify a `maxSize` and `BufferOverflowStrategy` (e.g., `DROP_OLDEST` or `ERROR`), and export buffer fill-level gauges.

failureModes.name: Missing Demand Replenishment (Pipeline Stall)
failureModes.description: A custom `Subscriber` requests `request(10)` in `onSubscribe` and forgets to call `request(1)` inside `onNext`, hanging the stream permanently after 10 items.
failureModes.mitigation: Use standard base classes (`BaseSubscriber`, `limitRate`) and test custom subscribers with Reactive Streams TCK.

failureModes.name: Blocking Call on Event-Loop Thread
failureModes.description: Executing a blocking JDBC query or `Thread.sleep()` inside `map()` stalls the shared Netty event-loop thread, halting `request(n)` signals for all other connections.
failureModes.mitigation: Isolate blocking work onto bounded `Schedulers.boundedElastic()` or virtual-thread executors, and enable BlockHound in CI.

failureModes.name: Protocol-Boundary Impedance Mismatch
failureModes.description: TCP/HTTP backpressure stops at a Kafka topic or Webhook boundary if the producer ignores `REQUEST_N` or `429` signals.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce explicit bounded queues, circuit breakers, or `onBackpressureDrop` + DLQ at every protocol boundary.

commonMistakes: Calling `request(Long.MAX_VALUE)` in `onSubscribe`, which disables backpressure completely and reverts to unbounded push.
Assuming `Flux.create()` automatically applies backpressure without configuring `OverflowStrategy` or registering `onRequest` callbacks.
Setting `flatMap` concurrency to default `256` on heavy 10 MB payloads, inadvertently buffering `256 * 10 MB = 2.5 GB` in flight.
Swallowing `MissingBackpressureException` instead of tuning prefetch rates or overflow strategies.
Confusing TCP flow control (byte-level) with application-level message backpressure when multiple logical streams multiplex over one connection.

sections.content:
## The idea

In a naive push pipeline, a fast producer calls `onNext(item)` as fast as it can generate data. If the consumer is slower, items pile up in an in-memory queue until memory is exhausted or latency degrades to minutes. Conversely, a naive pull pipeline (`next()` per item) pays a full round-trip latency tax on every single element.

**Reactive Streams backpressure** (JVM Spec / RSocket / HTTP/2 flow control) solves both problems with **dynamic push-pull**: the consumer tells the producer *how many* items it is ready to accept via `Subscription.request(n)`. The producer may push up to $n$ items asynchronously, and must pause once unfulfilled demand hits zero until more `request(k)` arrives.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a Reactor pipeline reading from a fast `Publisher` (50k msg/s) and writing to a slower database sink (10k msg/s) with `limitRate(64)`:

1. **Subscription**: The sink subscribes; `limitRate(64)` calls `subscription.request(64)` upstream (low-tide/high-tide batching).
2. **Push within budget**: The producer emits 64 items via `onNext(...)`, decrementing its atomic demand counter from `64` to `0`, then **pauses** without blocking any thread.
3. **Replenish at 75%**: Once the sink consumes 48 items (`75%` of 64), `limitRate` automatically issues `request(48)` upstream so the producer can refill the pipeline in parallel with the remaining 16 items.
4. **Sink slowdown**: If the DB stalls for 500 ms, the sink stops calling `onNext` completion; `request(48)` is never sent, demand stays at `0`, and upstream socket reads pause cleanly via Netty `autoRead = false`.

sections.content:
## Handling hot sources & overflow strategies

When a source cannot be slowed down (e.g., live sensor telemetry, UI clicks, UDP packets), `request(n)` cannot stop arrival. You must choose an explicit **backpressure overflow strategy** at the boundary:

- **`BUFFER` (bounded)**: Queue up to $N$ items; fail or spill if exceeded.
- **`DROP`**: Discard incoming items when demand is `0` (protects existing work).
- **`LATEST` (conflation)**: Keep only the most recent item per key/stream, overwriting stale unconsumed values—ideal for live stock quotes or progress bars.
- **`ERROR`**: Immediately signal `onError(MissingBackpressureException)` so the caller can fail fast or reconnect.

## Backpressure mechanisms across stacks

| Stack / Protocol | Flow-Control Primitive | Default Window / Batch | Granularity | Behavior at Zero Credit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Reactive Streams (JVM) | `Subscription.request(n)` | 256 (Reactor `SMALL_BUFFER_SIZE`) | Message count | Publisher stops calling `onNext` |
| RSocket | `REQUEST_N` frame | Configurable per stream | Message count | Network-transparent cross-process pause |
| gRPC / HTTP/2 | `WINDOW_UPDATE` frame | 65,535 bytes initial | Byte count | Sender blocks/suspends `DATA` frames |
| TCP | `SO_RCVBUF` + `WIN=0` | Kernel auto-tuned | Byte count | Kernel pauses `ACK` window; probes sent |
| Kafka Consumer | `poll()` + `pause()` | `max.poll.records` (500) | Record batch | Consumer stops fetching from broker |

## Failure modes

- **Unbounded buffer OOM**: Using `onBackpressureBuffer()` without a cap silently disables backpressure protection and crashes the JVM under sustained load.
- **Event-loop starvation**: Running blocking I/O on a Netty/Reactor event-loop thread halts `request(n)` processing for hundreds of concurrent streams.
- **Broken demand accounting**: Custom operators that miscount `Operators.addCap()` / `produced()` either hang at zero demand or violate the spec by over-emitting.
- **TCP head-of-line blocking**: Multiplexing multiple reactive streams onto a single TCP socket without stream-level credits allows one stalled stream to block all others.

## Production patterns & observability

- **End-to-end credit propagation**: Ensure Netty `autoRead=false` is wired to downstream `request(n)` so backpressure actually throttles the OS socket rather than just moving buffers around.
- **Monitor queue depth & drop counters**: Emit Prometheus gauges for bounded buffer occupancy and counters for `dropped_items_total` whenever `DROP` or `LATEST` triggers.
- **Use Reactor/RxJava TCK**: Validate any custom `Publisher` or `Subscriber` against the official Reactive Streams Technology Compatibility Kit (TCK) to catch subtle demand-race bugs.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Verify no operator in the pipeline calls `request(Long.MAX_VALUE)` or uses an unbounded `onBackpressureBuffer()`.
- [ ] Tune `limitRate(n)` and `flatMap(..., maxConcurrency)` to match downstream pool sizes and payload memory.
- [ ] Choose an explicit overflow strategy (`DROP`, `LATEST`, `ERROR`, or bounded `BUFFER`) at every hot/non-backpressured boundary.
- [ ] Keep event-loop threads 100% non-blocking; verify with BlockHound in CI.
- [ ] Instrument buffer fill ratios and dropped-message metrics to detect sustained backpressure before SLAs breach.

interviewProblems.title: Reactive Streams Backpressure
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Reactive Streams Backpressure. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Reactive Streams backpressure is a non-blocking, pull-based flow-control protocol where downstream consumers explicitly signal how many items (`request(n)`) they can process, preventing fast producers from overwhelming slow consumers.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Bounded Prefetch applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Slow Sink.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Slow Sink experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Always specify a `maxSize` and `BufferOverflowStrategy` (e.g., `DROP_OLDEST` or `ERROR`), and export buffer fill-level gauges.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Never bridge async producers and slow consumers with unbounded queues; use bounded `request(n)` demand signaling (e.g., Project Reactor, RSocket, gRPC HTTP/2 flow control) and define an explicit overflow strategy (`drop`, `latest`, or `error`) at non-backpressured boundaries.
Avoid trap: Calling `request(Long.MAX_VALUE)` in `onSubscribe`, which disables backpressure completely and reverts to unbounded push.
Avoid trap: Assuming `Flux.create()` automatically applies backpressure without configuring `OverflowStrategy` or registering `onRequest` callbacks.
When to reach for it: Streaming pipelines connecting fast ingress (Kafka, WebSockets, SSE, HTTP/2) to slower I/O sinks (PostgreSQL, Elasticsearch, ML inference).
When to reach for it: Non-blocking JVM or actor systems (Project Reactor, Akka/Pekko Streams, RxJava) where threads must never block on `queue.put()`.

putItTogether.title: Putting Reactive Streams Backpressure Together
putItTogether.summary: Never bridge async producers and slow consumers with unbounded queues; use bounded `request(n)` demand signaling (e.g., Project Reactor, RSocket, gRPC HTTP/2 flow control) and define an explicit overflow strategy (`drop`, `latest`, or `error`) at non-backpressured boundaries.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Reactive Streams Backpressure before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Using `bufferTimeout(500, 100ms)` with `limitRate(256)` propagates `request(n)` upstream, pausing Kafka partition polling automatically when Postgres slows down—holding heap usage flat at ~180 MB instead of OOMing.
